flashcards.q: What is DORA's operational definition of trunk-based development?
flashcards.a: Branches live under 24 hours and merge into a shared trunk at least daily; incomplete work ships dark behind feature flags rather than staying isolated on a long-lived branch.

flashcards.q: What are the three prerequisites for trunk-based development to actually work, not just in name?
flashcards.a: Fast/reliable CI, a merge queue that re-tests each PR against the actual current main (not branch-time main), and feature-flag discipline to decouple merged from released. Skip any one and it degrades to GitFlow with extra steps.

flashcards.q: What specific failure does a merge queue prevent that per-branch CI cannot catch?
flashcards.a: Two PRs each pass CI independently against main-at-branch-time, both merge back-to-back, and the COMBINATION breaks main in a way neither PR's own CI run ever saw. A merge queue re-tests serially against the actual resulting main state.

flashcards.q: Why do most trunk-based teams prefer squash-merge over merge commits?
flashcards.a: A linear, atomic-per-commit main is what makes git bisect and git blame reliable -- every point in history is a coherent, independently testable state. The cost is losing the true intra-feature development history.

flashcards.q: Why does a heavily-merged, long-lived-branch history make git bisect less reliable?
flashcards.a: Bisect's binary search assumes each candidate commit is a coherent, plausible state. A history with many merge commits has ancestry that splits and rejoins, so the midpoint can land inside a merge commit or a never-actually-deployed branch state.

flashcards.q: Why do teams now use git worktrees for running multiple AI coding agents against one repo?
flashcards.a: Each agent gets an isolated working directory and index while sharing one object database -- no lock contention, no context bleed between agents. A single shared checkout means one agent could read a file mid-edit by another.

flashcards.q: What does a naive git worktree setup miss when provisioning a new worktree for an agent?
flashcards.a: Untracked local state -- git worktree add only clones git-tracked files. .env files and other untracked config must be copied to each new worktree explicitly; worktree-aware agent CLIs automate this.

flashcards.q: Why is rebasing an already-pushed, shared branch a correctness problem, not just a style objection (Linus Torvalds's argument)?
flashcards.a: Rebase produces entirely new commit objects with new SHAs. Anyone who already pulled the pre-rebase commits now has a genuinely diverged history with no shared ancestor at those points -- their next pull duplicates commits or fails outright.

flashcards.q: When is GitFlow still the right choice over trunk-based development?
flashcards.a: Shrink-wrapped software with multiple supported versions live in the field simultaneously, needing independent patching via release/hotfix branches -- a problem shape trunk-based development doesn't address at all.

flashcards.q: What should you verify before trusting a git bisect result?
flashcards.a: That the repro script is deterministic -- rerun it 5x on the same commit first. A flaky repro makes bisect confidently converge on a random, wrong commit.

flashcards.q: Which 2026 IDE releases shipped native git worktree support timed to the AI-agent-per-worktree pattern?
flashcards.a: JetBrains IDEs in the 2026.1 release (March 2026); VS Code added worktree support in July 2025.

flashcards.q: A team calls itself trunk-based but branches live 1-2 weeks. What's the most likely root cause?
flashcards.a: Missing feature-flag discipline -- without a way to ship incomplete work dark, a long branch is the only place to hide unfinished features, reproducing GitFlow's merge-conflict pain under a different name.
